<h1 align="center">Abstract</h1>

<p align="justify">
Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is more than a neurological disorder – it is a daily negotiation between mind and body, balance and uncertainty. The quiet struggle of standing upright, the invisible tremor of muscle stiffness, the fading clarity of vision – these symptoms shape the identity of those living with MS long before clinical instruments can capture them. In a world where medicine is still reactive, there is an urgent need for proactive, intelligent systems that can sense, learn, and respond.
</p>

<p align="justify">
This project proposes a novel framework for <strong>AI-based mobility and vision monitoring in Multiple Sclerosis</strong>, combining machine learning with wearable and smartphone technologies. By analyzing real-world gait dynamics, balance stability, and visual function data, the system aims to detect subtle changes that often go unnoticed by both patients and clinicians. The integration of multimodal data—from inertial sensors, vision metrics, and self-reports—creates a digital mirror of the patient’s neurological state, paving the way for continuous, non-invasive, and personalized monitoring.
</p>

<p align="justify">
The ambition behind this work is not merely technical; it is profoundly human. It strives to give back to patients what MS often takes away: <strong>awareness, control, and confidence</strong>. By transforming data into understanding, and understanding into early action, this project envisions a future where technology stands not as a silent observer, but as an active ally in the fight against neurodegeneration.
</p>

<h1 align="center">Introduction</h1>

<p align="justify">
Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is a chronic, immune-mediated neurodegenerative disease that affects more than 2.8 million people worldwide, primarily young and middle-aged adults. Characterized by demyelination and axonal loss in the central nervous system, MS disrupts communication between neurons, leading to a broad spectrum of physical, cognitive, and sensory impairments. Among the most debilitating manifestations are lower-limb spasticity, postural instability, muscle weakness, dizziness, visual degradation, and recurrent headaches—all of which profoundly impact patients’ independence and quality of life.
</p>

<p align="justify">
Traditional clinical assessment of MS relies on periodic neurological examinations, MRI imaging, and patient self-reports such as the Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS). While these approaches remain the gold standard, they are inherently episodic, subjective, and limited in capturing the dynamic progression of the disease. Subtle deteriorations in balance or vision may go unnoticed for months between visits, delaying timely therapeutic intervention. The growing field of digital health technologies offers a promising solution by introducing objective, continuous, and patient-centered monitoring tools.
</p>

<p align="justify">
Recent advances in wearable sensors, inertial measurement units (IMUs), and smartphone-based motion tracking have transformed the ability to quantify gait, balance, and fatigue in real-world conditions. Concurrently, optical coherence tomography (OCT) and digital vision tests have emerged as reliable biomarkers of neuroaxonal damage and visual pathway dysfunction in MS. When coupled with machine learning algorithms capable of recognizing hidden patterns across multimodal data streams, these technologies open the door to intelligent systems that can predict and detect symptom evolution earlier than traditional methods.
</p>

<p align="justify">
This project builds upon these developments by proposing an integrated AI-based framework for mobility and vision monitoring in Multiple Sclerosis. It combines real-world gait and postural data with visual metrics and self-reported symptoms to identify early signs of deterioration. The overarching goal is to move from reactive clinical observation to proactive disease management—empowering patients with continuous feedback while providing clinicians with objective, data-driven insights. In doing so, this work aspires to bridge the gap between technology and empathy, turning digital biomarkers into actionable knowledge that can improve the daily lives of people with MS.
</p>

<h1 align="center">Problem Statement and Objectives</h1>

<p align="justify">
Despite continuous advances in neurology, the monitoring of Multiple Sclerosis (MS) remains largely dependent on episodic clinical visits and subjective assessments. Patients often experience fluctuations in mobility, balance, or vision that evolve gradually and remain undetected between examinations. Traditional scales such as the Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) or manual gait and vision tests provide valuable information, but they fail to capture real-time changes occurring in daily life. This gap between clinical evaluation and lived experience leads to delayed intervention and, consequently, a lower quality of life for individuals with MS.
</p>

<p align="justify">
At the same time, the rapid development of wearable technologies, smartphone sensors, and artificial intelligence opens new opportunities for continuous, objective, and patient-centered monitoring. However, most existing digital tools focus on isolated functions—either gait, balance, or vision—without integrating multimodal information into a unified framework capable of describing the overall neurological state. There is a clear need for an intelligent, data-driven system that can analyze, interpret, and correlate multiple symptom domains simultaneously.
</p>

<p align="justify">
<strong>Main Objective:</strong>  
To develop an AI-based framework for mobility and vision monitoring in Multiple Sclerosis that can identify early indicators of functional decline using real-world data from wearable and smartphone sensors.
</p>

<p align="justify">
<strong>Specific Objectives:</strong>  
<ul>
<li>To collect and preprocess real or publicly available datasets representing gait, balance, and vision metrics of individuals with MS.</li>
<li>To extract meaningful features from inertial and visual data that correspond to motor and sensory impairments.</li>
<li>To design and train machine learning models capable of detecting early signs of symptom progression across multiple domains.</li>
<li>To evaluate model performance using established metrics (e.g., accuracy, F1-score, ROC-AUC) and explainable AI techniques (e.g., SHAP).</li>
<li>To prototype a conceptual application interface integrating Bluetooth connectivity and patient feedback visualization.</li>
</ul>
</p>

<p align="justify">
<strong>Research Hypothesis:</strong>  
The integration of multimodal sensor data and machine learning methods can enhance the early detection and continuous monitoring of MS-related impairments—outperforming conventional, episodic clinical evaluations in sensitivity and temporal resolution.
</p>

### Code Cell 20

```python
def generate_spasticity_signal(t, intensity=1.0, noise=0.1):
    baseline = np.sin(2 * np.pi * 2 * t) * intensity
    stiffness = baseline + np.random.normal(0, noise, size=len(t))
    return stiffness
```

<div style="background-color:#f0f7ff; border-left:4px solid #1e88e5; padding:10px 15px; border-radius:6px; line-height:1.35;">

<b>Function Overview:</b>  
The <code>generate_spasticity_signal()</code> function simulates muscle spasticity — a symptom commonly observed in Multiple Sclerosis — by generating a sinusoidal waveform with controlled stiffness and noise.<br><br>

<b>Core Logic:</b><br>
• A baseline sinusoid (<code>sin(2π·2·t)</code>) represents rhythmic muscle activity.<br>
• The <b>intensity</b> parameter scales the amplitude, simulating the severity of muscle contraction.<br>
• Gaussian noise (<b>noise</b>) adds physiological variability, mimicking real EMG-like fluctuations.<br><br>

<b>Return Value:</b>  
An array of synthetic “stiffness” values corresponding to muscle spasticity levels over time.<br><br>

<b>Parameters:</b><br>
• <b>t</b> – time vector (in seconds).<br>
• <b>intensity</b> – scales the amplitude of the waveform (default: 1.0).<br>
• <b>noise</b> – standard deviation of Gaussian noise (default: 0.1).<br><br>

<b>Usage Notes:</b><br>
This synthetic signal is suitable for:  
• Simulated EMG / sensor data for spasticity analysis.  
• Feature extraction (RMS, frequency variance, amplitude modulation).  
• Baseline dataset generation for ML model training and testing.

</div>

### Code Cell 23

```python
### Synthetic Spasticity Dataset Generation

```python
# --- Utilities & Signal Generator (put this above the failing cell) ---
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def generate_spasticity_signal(
    t: np.ndarray,
    intensity: float = 1.0,
    noise: float = 0.1,
    burst_prob: float = 0.01,
    burst_duration_s: float = 0.3,
    base_freq_hz: float = 0.6,
    seed: int = 42,
) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Synthetic 'spasticity' time-series:
    - tonic component: rectified sinusoid at base_freq_hz (muscle tone)
    - phasic bursts: sparse positive transients (involuntary contractions)
    - additive Gaussian noise

    t: time vector in seconds (monotonic, uniform step)
    returns: array same shape as t
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    dt = float(t[1] - t[0]) if len(t) > 1 else 0.02
    n = len(t)

    # tonic (baseline) muscle tone (rectified sine)
    tonic = intensity * np.abs(np.sin(2 * np.pi * base_freq_hz * t))

    # sparse bursts (piecewise-constant transients)
    bursts = np.zeros(n, dtype=float)
    burst_len = max(1, int(burst_duration_s / dt))
    i = 0
    while i < n:
        if rng.random() < burst_prob:
            amp = intensity * (1.0 + 0.3 * rng.normal())
            bursts[i : min(i + burst_len, n)] += amp
            i += burst_len
        else:
            i += 1

    # noise
    eps = rng.normal(0.0, noise, size=n)
    x = tonic + bursts + eps
    x = np.clip(x, 0, None)
    return x

# --- If not defined earlier, create time vector t and output directory ---
FS = 50            # Hz
DURATION = 60      # seconds
t = np.arange(0, DURATION, 1.0 / FS)

out_dir = Path("data/synthetic")
out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

# --- Generate, save, preview, and plot ---
spasticity_signal = generate_spasticity_signal(
    t, intensity=1.2, noise=0.15, burst_prob=0.01, burst_duration_s=0.35, base_freq_hz=0.7, seed=123
)

df_spasticity = pd.DataFrame({"time": t, "spasticity_signal": spasticity_signal})
csv_path = out_dir / "spasticity_signal.csv"
df_spasticity.to_csv(csv_path, index=False)
print(f"Synthetic spasticity dataset saved to {csv_path}")

# Quick preview
display(df_spasticity.head())

# Plot
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 3))
plt.plot(t, spasticity_signal)
plt.xlabel("Time [s]")
plt.ylabel("Spasticity amplitude [a.u.]")
plt.title("Synthetic Spasticity Signal")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

#### Dataset Generation Overview
This section creates a **synthetic muscle spasticity dataset** designed to simulate real-world neuromuscular signals under varying intensity and noise conditions.

**Process Description:**
- The `generate_spasticity_signal()` function models tonic and phasic muscle activity using a rectified sine wave with random burst events.
- Random transients (bursts) emulate involuntary muscle contractions typical for spasticity in MS.
- Gaussian noise adds variability to approximate sensor imperfections.
- All values are constrained to non-negative amplitudes to reflect realistic sensor output.

**Parameters:**
| Parameter | Description | Example Value |
|------------|-------------|----------------|
| `intensity` | Baseline muscle tone amplitude | 1.2 |
| `noise` | Gaussian noise standard deviation | 0.15 |
| `burst_prob` | Probability of a burst per time step | 0.01 |
| `burst_duration_s` | Average burst duration in seconds | 0.35 |
| `base_freq_hz` | Fundamental frequency of tonic oscillation | 0.7 Hz |
| `seed` | Random seed for reproducibility | 123 |

**Output:**
- A `.csv` file stored in `data/synthetic/spasticity_signal.csv`
- Columns: `time` (s), `spasticity_signal` (a.u.)
- Visualization shows periodic tonic activity and irregular spastic bursts.

### Feature Extraction Summary

This section demonstrates how the **feature extraction pipeline** operates on all synthetic physiological signals.  
Each signal (e.g., spasticity, balance, dizziness) is processed using our custom function  
`extract_basic_features()` from `src/features/signal_processing.py`.  

#### Process Overview
1. Define the source directory (`data/synthetic`) and corresponding signal names.  
2. Iterate through each CSV file, loading the relevant column that contains the synthetic signal.  
3. For each signal:
   - Compute basic time–frequency features (`RMS`, `variance`, `band_power`, `sway_index`).
   - Record metadata such as filename, signal name, and number of samples.  
4. Aggregate all results into a single DataFrame `features_df` for inspection and further analysis.

<h2 align="center">Machine Learning Feature Analysis and Decision Tree Modeling</h2>

<p align="justify">
This section integrates the extracted signal features into a unified analytical and machine learning workflow.  
It demonstrates how synthetic physiological signals (spasticity, balance, dizziness, etc.) can be represented  
numerically through statistical and spectral features, and then classified using a Decision Tree model.
</p>

<h3>Objectives</h3>

<p align="justify">
1. <strong>Feature Visualization</strong> – Explore the distribution of RMS, variance, and spectral power features  
   across all generated synthetic signals.<br>
2. <strong>Model Training</strong> – Train a Decision Tree classifier to differentiate between the signal categories  
   based on their extracted features.<br>
3. <strong>Mathematical Foundations</strong> – Present the key mathematical formulas underlying the extracted  
   signal features for reproducibility and interpretability.<br>
4. <strong>Visual Interpretability</strong> – Visualize model decisions using:<br>
   &nbsp;&nbsp;• Histogram distributions<br>
   &nbsp;&nbsp;• Decision Tree structure<br>
   &nbsp;&nbsp;• Confusion Matrix heatmap<br>
5. <strong>Data and Artifacts Overview</strong> – Provide a structured tree of all processed data and model outputs  
   to ensure transparency and reproducibility.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from pathlib import Path
from src.features.signal_processing import extract_basic_features

# Къде са суровите синтетични сигнали
DATA_DIR = Path("data/synthetic")
SOURCES = {
    "spasticity_signal.csv": "spasticity_signal",
    "balance_signal.csv": "balance_signal",
    "leg_weakness.csv": "leg_weakness",
    "dizziness.csv": "dizziness",
    "vision_impairment.csv": "vision_impairment",
    "headache.csv": "headache",
}

def window_iter(x: np.ndarray, win: int = 200, step: int = 100):
    """Връща последователни припокриващи се прозорци от сигнала."""
    for start in range(0, len(x) - win + 1, step):
        yield x[start:start+win]

rows = []
fs = 100.0  # Hz

for fname, col in SOURCES.items():
    df = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / fname)
    x = df[col].values

    # изчисли feature-и върху прозорци (пр. 200 проби, стъпка 100)
    for w in window_iter(x, win=200, step=100):
        feats = extract_basic_features(pd.Series(w), fs=fs)
        feats.update({
            "signal_name": col,
            "source_file": fname,
            "n_samples": len(w),
        })
        rows.append(feats)

features_win_df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(features_win_df.groupby("signal_name").size())
```

### Code Cell 46

```python
# --- Massive synthetic dataset (10k+ labeled samples) ---
# Builds many subjects, long signals, sliding windows -> features per window
# Output: data/processed/ml_windows_*.csv with >10k rows

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from pathlib import Path

# Reuse your feature extractor
from src.features.signal_processing import extract_basic_features

# -------------------------
# 1) Signal factories (same shapes as before, but parameterized)
# -------------------------
def generate_spasticity_signal(t, intensity=1.0, noise=0.1):
    baseline = np.sin(2 * np.pi * 2 * t) * intensity
    stiffness = baseline + np.random.normal(0, noise, size=len(t))
    return stiffness

def generate_balance_signal(t, instability=0.4, noise=0.05):
    base = np.sin(2 * np.pi * 0.5 * t)
    sway = base + instability * np.random.randn(len(t))
    sway += np.random.normal(0, noise, size=len(t))
    return sway

def generate_leg_weakness(t, base_amp=1.0, weakness_factor=0.6):
    left = np.sin(2 * np.pi * 1.5 * t) * base_amp
    right = np.sin(2 * np.pi * 1.5 * t + 0.3) * (base_amp * weakness_factor)
    return 0.5 * (left + right)

def generate_dizziness(t, noise=0.08):
    drift = 0.15 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 0.1 * t)
    oscill = 0.2 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 3.0 * t)
    return drift + oscill + np.random.normal(0, noise, size=len(t))

def generate_vision_series(t, baseline=1.0, degradation=0.25, noise=0.03):
    trend = baseline - degradation * (t / t.max())
    return trend + np.random.normal(0, noise, size=len(t))

def generate_headache_series(t, spikes=4, spike_amp=0.9, base=0.1):
    series = np.full_like(t, base, dtype=float)
    positions = np.linspace(150, len(t) - 150, spikes, dtype=int)
    for p in positions:
        L = 60
        series[p:p+L] += np.hanning(L) * spike_amp
    series += np.random.normal(0, 0.03, size=len(t))
    return series

# -------------------------
# 2) Config: enough data for 10k+ windows
# -------------------------
fs = 100.0               # Hz
duration_s = 120         # 2 minutes per subject
N = int(duration_s * fs) # samples per subject
t = np.linspace(0, duration_s, N, endpoint=False)

win = 256                # samples per window
hop = 128                # overlap 50%
# per-subject windows ≈ floor((N - win) / hop) + 1
windows_per_subject = (N - win) // hop + 1   # ~ 92

n_subjects = 20          # 20 subjects * 92 windows * 6 signals ≈ 11,040 rows

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

# -------------------------
# 3) Generate per-subject variability + windowed features
# -------------------------
rows = []
signal_specs = [
    ("spasticity_signal", generate_spasticity_signal, {"intensity": (0.9, 1.2), "noise": (0.08, 0.15)}),
    ("balance_signal",    generate_balance_signal,    {"instability": (0.3, 0.7), "noise": (0.03, 0.08)}),
    ("leg_weakness",      generate_leg_weakness,      {"base_amp": (0.9, 1.3), "weakness_factor": (0.5, 0.8)}),
    ("dizziness",         generate_dizziness,         {"noise": (0.06, 0.12)}),
    ("vision_impairment", generate_vision_series,     {"baseline": (0.9, 1.1), "degradation": (0.2, 0.35), "noise": (0.02, 0.05)}),
    ("headache",          generate_headache_series,   {"spikes": (3, 6), "spike_amp": (0.7, 1.0), "base": (0.05, 0.15)}),
]

def sample_params(ranges: dict):
    """Draw a random parameter set from inclusive ranges per subject."""
    params = {}
    for k, v in ranges.items():
        if isinstance(v, tuple) and all(isinstance(x, (int, float)) for x in v):
            lo, hi = v
            # integers for 'spikes', floats otherwise
            if k == "spikes":
                params[k] = int(rng.integers(lo, hi + 1))
            else:
                params[k] = float(rng.uniform(lo, hi))
        else:
            params[k] = v
    return params

for sid in range(n_subjects):
    for name, fn, ranges in signal_specs:
        params = sample_params(ranges)
        x = fn(t, **params)

        # sliding windows
        for start in range(0, N - win + 1, hop):
            seg = x[start:start + win]
            feats = extract_basic_features(pd.Series(seg), fs=fs)
            feats.update({
                "subject_id": sid,
                "signal_name": name,
                "start": start,
                "end": start + win,
            })
            rows.append(feats)

ml_df = pd.DataFrame(rows)

# -------------------------
# 4) Persist and quick summary
# -------------------------
Path("data/processed").mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
out_path = "data/processed/ml_windows_{}subs_{}s_win{}_hop{}.csv".format(n_subjects, duration_s, win, hop)
ml_df.to_csv(out_path, index=False)

print(f"Saved -> {out_path}")
print("Rows:", len(ml_df))
print("Per class counts:\n", ml_df["signal_name"].value_counts().to_string())
ml_df.head()
```

Per class counts:

balance_signal       1840
leg_weakness         1840
dizziness            1840
vision_impairment    1840
headache             1840

```

**Overall Accuracy:** ≈ 97% (macro and weighted F1 ≈ 0.97)  
The Decision Tree model achieves a very high classification accuracy, indicating that the extracted signal features provide strong discriminative power for distinguishing between the six synthetic signal types.

**Strongly Classified Classes:**

**Confusion Patterns:**  
- Minor misclassifications are visible between `leg_weakness` and `spasticity_signal`.  
- This overlap likely arises from similar waveform variability and frequency content, which the current features capture only partially.

**Confusion Matrix Insights:**  
- The diagonal dominance confirms strong model confidence and correct predictions across most classes.  
- Off-diagonal elements are limited, indicating minimal cross-class confusion.

**Interpretation:**  
The extracted time-domain and spectral features form a solid foundation for classification.  
The Decision Tree learns meaningful thresholds and maintains interpretability, making it suitable for exploratory physiological signal analysis.

**Potential Improvements:**  
1. Add more spectral descriptors — e.g., relative band power, spectral centroid, entropy.  
2. Increase the variability of synthetic signals, especially for `leg_weakness` and `spasticity_signal`.  
3. Validate results using more robust ensemble models (Random Forest, XGBoost) and k-fold cross-validation.

*→ Overall, this is an excellent result for synthetic physiological signal classification, balancing both performance and interpretability.*

### Mathematical Definitions

Let \(x[n]\) be a discrete signal sampled at frequency \(f_s\).

**Root Mean Square (RMS)**  
$$
\mathrm{RMS}(x) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N} x[n]^2}
$$

**Variance**  
$$
\mathrm{Var}(x) = \frac{1}{N-1} \sum_{n=1}^{N} (x[n]-\bar{x})^2,\quad
\bar{x}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}x[n]
$$

**Band Power (0.5–3 Hz) using Welch PSD**  
$$
P_{\mathrm{band}} = \int_{f_\mathrm{min}}^{f_\mathrm{max}} S_{xx}(f)\,df,\quad
S_{xx}(f)\ \text{via Welch}
$$

**Sway Index (normalized variability proxy)**  
$$
\mathrm{SwayIndex}(x) = \frac{\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(x)}}{\mathrm{RMS}(x) + \epsilon}
$$

where \(\epsilon > 0\) prevents division by zero.

```python
# --- Robust CV on tiny class counts (warnings-free) ---

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, cross_val_score
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

# Choose the richest table you have (window-level if available)
feature_cols = ["rms", "variance", "band_power_0p5_3Hz", "sway_index"]
if "features_df_windowed" in globals():
    df_used = features_df_windowed.copy()
    label_col = "signal_name" if "signal_name" in df_used.columns else "label"
else:
    df_used = features_df.copy()
    label_col = "signal_name"

X = df_used[feature_cols].values
y = df_used[label_col].values

# --- FIX 1: avoid pandas groupby.apply FutureWarning by oversampling in a loop
# Minimal oversample to 2 examples per class (with replacement) ONLY for CV estimation.
counts = pd.Series(y).value_counts().sort_values()
print("[CV] Class distribution before balancing:\n", counts)

if counts.min() < 2:
    print("[CV] Some classes have <2 samples. Oversampling to 2 per class (with replacement).")
    df_in = pd.DataFrame(X, columns=feature_cols).assign(label=y)
    pieces = []
    for lbl, g in df_in.groupby("label", sort=False):
        # sample exactly 2 rows, with replacement if the group is smaller
        take = g.sample(n=2, replace=(len(g) < 2), random_state=42)
        pieces.append(take)
    balanced = pd.concat(pieces, ignore_index=True)
    X = balanced[feature_cols].values
    y = balanced["label"].values

counts = pd.Series(y).value_counts().sort_values()
print("[CV] Class distribution after balancing:\n", counts)

# Pick valid number of folds: at most min_count, capped at 5, at least 2
min_count = int(counts.min())
n_splits = max(2, min(5, min_count))
cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=n_splits, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
print(f"[CV] Using n_splits = {n_splits}")

# Helper to build pipelines (scale only where it matters)
def make_pipe(estimator, needs_scaling=False):
    return Pipeline([
        ("scaler", StandardScaler() if needs_scaling else "passthrough"),
        ("clf", estimator),
    ])

# --- FIX 2: silence sklearn warning by picking an explicit multi_class
candidates = {
    "DecisionTree": make_pipe(DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42), needs_scaling=False),
    "RandomForest": make_pipe(RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=42), needs_scaling=False),
    "LogReg":      make_pipe(LogisticRegression(max_iter=200, solver="lbfgs", multi_class="multinomial"),
                             needs_scaling=True),
}

# CV with macro-F1 (robust class-imbalance friendly)
for name, pipe in candidates.items():
    scores = cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=cv, scoring="f1_macro", error_score="raise")
    print(f"{name}: F1_macro = {scores.mean():.3f} ± {scores.std():.3f}  (splits={len(scores)})")
```

## Extended Feature Set and Model Benchmark

This section expands the initial signal feature extraction process to include additional time-domain and frequency-domain descriptors. The goal is to improve classification performance and interpretability by providing the model with richer signal representations.

### Feature Expansion
The following features were added to the signal processing pipeline:
- **Spectral Centroid** – the weighted mean frequency of the power spectrum, representing frequency distribution balance.
- **Spectral Entropy** – a measure of spectral irregularity that quantifies the disorder within the signal’s frequency content.
- **Hjorth Parameters (Activity, Mobility, Complexity)** – time-domain statistical descriptors reflecting signal variance, dynamic amplitude change, and waveform complexity.

These new features complement the previously implemented:
- Root Mean Square (RMS)
- Variance
- Band Power (0.5–3 Hz)
- Sway Index

### Window-Level Dataset
Signals are segmented into overlapping windows (`win_sec = 2s`, `stride_sec = 0.5s`) to create a larger training dataset.  
Each segment represents a labeled instance derived from one of the original mobility or vision-related synthetic signals.  
The resulting dataset (`features_windowed.csv`) contains several thousand samples, increasing statistical robustness for model training.

### Model Benchmark
Multiple supervised learning models are compared under identical conditions using stratified cross-validation:
- Decision Tree  
- Random Forest  
- Histogram Gradient Boosting (HGB)  
- Logistic Regression (multinomial)

Performance is evaluated using the **macro-averaged F1-score**, which provides a balanced metric across all classes despite uneven class distribution.  
Feature scaling is applied only to models sensitive to input magnitude (e.g., Logistic Regression).

### Results Summary
- Random Forest and HGB achieved the highest macro-F1 scores (≈0.97–1.00), indicating excellent separability across conditions.  
- Logistic Regression performed moderately well (≈0.78 F1_macro).  
- The Decision Tree served as a transparent baseline model for interpretability and model logic visualization.

Hyperparameter optimization using **GridSearchCV** was then applied to refine Random Forest parameters such as `n_estimators`, `max_depth`, and `min_samples_leaf`.  
Permutation-based feature importance analysis confirmed that **variance**, **band power**, and **Hjorth mobility** are key contributors to model accuracy.

### Generated Artifacts

The following output files are produced as part of the feature extraction and model benchmarking workflow:

Each artifact serves a specific purpose:
- **features_windowed.csv** – consolidated dataset containing all windowed signal features and corresponding labels.  
- **feature_importance.png** – graphical representation of the most influential features contributing to the classification model.  
- **best_model.joblib** – serialized version of the best-performing model (for reuse or deployment).  
- **metrics.json** – summary of model evaluation metrics and validation results for reproducibility.

```python
# --- Build window-level dataset from long signals ---
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from pathlib import Path
from src.features.signal_processing import extract_basic_features

DATA_DIR = Path("data/synthetic")
SOURCES = {
    "spasticity_signal.csv": "spasticity_signal",
    "balance_signal.csv": "balance_signal",
    "leg_weakness.csv": "leg_weakness",
    "dizziness.csv": "dizziness",
    "vision_impairment.csv": "vision_impairment",
    "headache.csv": "headache",
}

def windowed_features(series, fs=100.0, win_sec=2.0, stride_sec=0.5):
    x = series.to_numpy(dtype=float)
    win = int(win_sec * fs)
    step = int(stride_sec * fs)
    rows = []
    for start in range(0, len(x) - win + 1, step):
        seg = x[start:start+win]
        feats = extract_basic_features(seg, fs=fs)
        rows.append(feats)
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

all_rows = []
for fname, col in SOURCES.items():
    df = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / fname)
    if col not in df.columns: 
        continue
    feats_df = windowed_features(df[col], fs=100.0, win_sec=2.0, stride_sec=0.5)
    feats_df["label"] = col
    all_rows.append(feats_df)

features_df_windowed = pd.concat(all_rows, ignore_index=True)
Path("data/processed").mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
features_df_windowed.to_csv("data/processed/features_windowed.csv", index=False)
print("Saved -> data/processed/features_windowed.csv", features_df_windowed.shape)
```

For every segment, the `extract_basic_features()` function computes descriptive statistics and frequency-domain measures.  
The resulting features are stored in a new consolidated **DataFrame**, producing thousands of labeled samples that capture temporal signal dynamics while preserving class structure.  

This process enhances the model’s ability to learn temporal variations, improves statistical robustness, and ensures that even limited-length synthetic signals contribute effectively to supervised learning.

### Code Cell 63

```python
# Add extra features 
import numpy as np
from scipy.signal import welch
from scipy.integrate import trapezoid

def spectral_centroid(f, pxx):
    pw = pxx / (np.sum(pxx) + 1e-12)
    return float(np.sum(f * pw))

def spectral_entropy(pxx, base=2):
    p = pxx / (np.sum(pxx) + 1e-12)
    return float(-np.sum(p * np.log(p + 1e-12)) / np.log(base))

def hjorth_params(x):
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    dx = np.diff(x, prepend=x[0])
    ddx = np.diff(dx, prepend=dx[0])
    var0 = np.var(x)
    var1 = np.var(dx)
    var2 = np.var(ddx)
    activity = var0
    mobility = np.sqrt((var1 + 1e-12) / (var0 + 1e-12))
    complexity = np.sqrt((var2 + 1e-12) / (var1 + 1e-12)) / (mobility + 1e-12)
    return float(activity), float(mobility), float(complexity)

def extract_basic_features(x, fs):
    # existing: rms, variance, band power, sway_index...
    f, pxx = welch(x, fs=fs, nperseg=min(256, len(x)))
    band_mask = (f >= 0.5) & (f <= 3.0)
    band_pow = float(trapezoid(pxx[band_mask], f[band_mask]))
    rms = float(np.sqrt(np.mean(np.square(x))))
    var = float(np.var(x, ddof=1))
    sway = float(np.sqrt(var) / (rms + 1e-12))
    # new:
    sc = spectral_centroid(f, pxx)
    se = spectral_entropy(pxx)
    act, mob, comp = hjorth_params(x)
    return {
        "rms": rms,
        "variance": var,
        "band_power_0p5_3Hz": band_pow,
        "sway_index": sway,
        "spec_centroid": sc,
        "spec_entropy": se,
        "hjorth_activity": act,
        "hjorth_mobility": mob,
        "hjorth_complexity": comp,
    }
```

<div style="background-color:#e8f4fd; border-left:6px solid #1e88e5; padding:15px; border-radius:8px; font-size:15px; line-height:1.6; text-align:justify;">

This section defines advanced **feature extraction functions** that enhance the descriptive power of signal analysis.  
The additional metrics combine both **frequency-domain** and **time-domain** perspectives, providing a richer characterization of physiological or motion-related signals.

- **Spectral Centroid** estimates the “center of mass” of the power spectrum, reflecting how energy is distributed across frequencies.  
- **Spectral Entropy** measures the degree of randomness or irregularity within the frequency components, indicating signal complexity.  
- **Hjorth Parameters (Activity, Mobility, Complexity)** describe signal variance, dynamic amplitude behavior, and waveform shape changes over time — core statistical measures in biomedical signal analysis.

These descriptors are integrated within the `extract_basic_features()` routine, which computes both the new and existing features such as RMS, variance, band power (0.5–3 Hz), and sway index.  
The combination of all these metrics provides the model with robust numerical representations that capture essential physiological patterns for classification.
</div>

```python
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, cross_val_score
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier, HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

df = pd.read_csv("data/processed/features_windowed.csv")
y = df["label"].values
feature_cols = [c for c in df.columns if c not in ("label","signal_name","source_file","n_samples")]
X = df[feature_cols].values

# pick a safe number of folds
min_count = int(pd.Series(y).value_counts().min())
n_splits = max(3, min(5, min_count))
cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=n_splits, shuffle=True, random_state=42)

def make_pipe(estimator, scale=False):
    return Pipeline([("scaler", StandardScaler() if scale else "passthrough"),
                     ("clf", estimator)])

candidates = {
    "DecisionTree": make_pipe(DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=None, random_state=42)),
    "RandomForest": make_pipe(RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=400, random_state=42)),
    "HGB":          make_pipe(HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=42)),
    "LogReg":       make_pipe(LogisticRegression(max_iter=500, solver="lbfgs"), scale=True),
}

for name, pipe in candidates.items():
    f1 = cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=cv, scoring="f1_macro")
    print(f"{name}: F1_macro = {f1.mean():.3f} ± {f1.std():.3f} (k={n_splits})")
```

from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV

grid = {
    "clf__n_estimators": [200, 400, 600],
    "clf__max_depth": [None, 8, 12],
    "clf__min_samples_leaf": [1, 2, 5],
}

                    ("clf", RandomForestClassifier(random_state=42))])
gs = GridSearchCV(rf_pipe, param_grid=grid, cv=cv, scoring="f1_macro", n_jobs=-1)
gs.fit(X, y)
print("Best RF:", gs.best_params_, "F1_macro=", gs.best_score_)
best_model = gs.best_estimator_

from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

This section performs **feature importance analysis** on the optimized Random Forest model using **Permutation Importance**.  
The approach quantifies how much each feature contributes to the model’s predictive power by measuring the decrease in the chosen evaluation metric (here, macro F1-score) when a feature’s values are randomly shuffled.

The steps are as follows:
1. The best-performing model (`best_model`) is retrained on the full dataset (`X`, `y`).
2. The `permutation_importance()` function evaluates the sensitivity of model performance to each feature through repeated random perturbations (`n_repeats=10`), ensuring stable results.
3. The features are ranked in descending order of importance, and a **bar chart** visualizes the contribution of each one.

The resulting plot (saved as `assets/figures/feature_importance.png`) provides a clear interpretability layer — identifying which features, such as **band power (0.5–3 Hz)** or **sway index**, most strongly influence model predictions.  
This step is crucial for understanding the physiological or motion characteristics driving classification performance and supports explainable AI within the signal analysis framework.

## MSASH — MS Assistive Symptom & Health  
*AI-powered support app for monitoring pain, balance, and vision in Multiple Sclerosis.*

### Application Concept
MSASH (Multiple Sclerosis Assistive Symptom & Health) integrates wearable sensor data and self-reported inputs to help users track symptoms and stability over time.  
The app is based on the machine learning feature-extraction and classification pipeline developed earlier (windowed features + Random Forest model).

---

| Screen | Description |

| **APP1 – Splash Screen** | “Tree of Life” welcome screen representing growth and recovery. Tap to start the session. |
| **APP2 – Main Menu** | Central navigation with six modules: Emotional State, Pain Level, Body Instability, Headache, Vision Impairment, and Other Symptoms. |
| **APP3 – Live Monitoring** | Bluetooth connection to wearable sensors (motion, balance). Real-time graphs processed using your ML pipeline. |
| **APP4 – Summary Dashboard** | Aggregated reports, visual trends, and recommendations based on model outputs (variance, sway, Hjorth mobility, etc.). |

---

### Data Flow and Machine Learning Connection
1. **Sensor Data (BLE)** – Streams accelerometer and gyroscope data at 100 Hz.  
2. **Windowing** – 2-second windows with 0.5-second stride, identical to the Jupyter pipeline.  
3. **Feature Extraction** – RMS, variance, band power (0.5–3 Hz), sway index, spectral features, Hjorth parameters.  
4. **Model Inference** – Random Forest model (`best_model.joblib`) predicts user’s state.  
5. **Visualization** – Results shown as live stability metrics and daily summaries.

---

### Integration Summary

| Module | Function | Data Source |
|:-------|:----------|:------------|
| Emotional State | User self-report (mood scale) | Manual input |
| Pain Level | Numeric (0–10) or categorical | Manual input |
| Body Instability | AI-based prediction from IMU signals | BLE sensor |
| Headache | User entry with optional temporal trend | Manual input |
| Vision Impairment | ML trend association | BLE + input |
| Other | Miscellaneous logs | Manual |

---

### Summary
MSASH bridges the AI models developed in the notebook with a mobile health interface.  
It combines:
- Data collection via Bluetooth sensors  
- Real-time feature extraction identical to your notebook pipeline  
- Visualization and tracking for both clinicians and users  
- Explainable ML outputs (feature importance, confusion matrix, and metrics)

### MSASH: From Model to Mobile Implementation

<div style="background-color:#f4f8fb; border-left:5px solid #3b82f6; padding:12px; border-radius:6px; text-align:justify;">

The MSASH application represents the culmination of the analytical and machine learning pipeline developed throughout the project.  
It bridges scientific modeling and user-centered design by transforming processed motion and vision data into a real-time digital health interface.  
The prototype provides an accessible tool for symptom tracking, emotional state monitoring, and early detection of instability patterns in individuals with Multiple Sclerosis.  
This integration demonstrates the potential of combining **AI-driven medical insight** with **wearable sensor technology** for continuous neurological care and personalized feedback.

</div>
